text:
**Recommendation.** Adopt short, class-specific retention with automatic enforcement: application logs 30 days, infrastructure logs 30 days (raw IPs) with only truncated or hashed derivatives beyond that if needed, audit logs 13 months in a separate, minimal, append-only store, and database backups 35 days instead of 90. Honour the 30-day deletion promise by deleting live data on time and by making backups expire quickly enough that the residual exposure is bounded, disclosed in the contract, and never restored without re-applying deletions. This is a design proposal, not legal advice. Have counsel review the contract wording and the audit-log justification, which are the two places where judgement calls matter most.

**Application logs: 30 days.** These carry user identifiers and sometimes free text, so they are personal data and the highest-risk class, because free text is uncontrolled and may contain anything. Their purpose is debugging and incident response, and operational debugging rarely needs more than a few weeks. Thirty days also means they age out inside the contractual deletion window without any per-customer log surgery. Engineering work that supports this: stop logging free text by default, redact or hash user identifiers where a stable pseudonym suffices, and tag log lines with a tenant ID so that an emergency purge is possible.

**Infrastructure logs: 30 days for raw IPs.** IP addresses are personal data under GDPR when the holder can reasonably link them to a person (the CJEU's Breyer ruling treats even dynamic IPs this way where legal means of identification exist), so the safe assumption is that they are. The purpose is security monitoring and abuse investigation. If you want longer trend data, truncate the last octet (or hash with a rotating salt) before the 30-day mark and keep only that form. Note that truncation reduces risk but is pseudonymisation or partial anonymisation at best; do not call it anonymous without analysis.

**Audit logs: 13 months, separate store.** Audit logs record security-relevant events: logins, permission changes, admin actions, data exports, deletions. The security lead's request for at least a year is reasonable (13 months lets you compare year over year and covers an annual cycle plus slack). The justification is the security of processing and accountability, and likely legitimate interests; it should be documented, not assumed. Keep this store narrow: actor ID, action, object ID, timestamp, source IP if essential, and no free text and no payload contents. The narrower the content, the easier it is to defend retention beyond 30 days. State the limit plainly: a year-plus of retention is defensible for security purposes, but it is longer than the deletion promise, so the contract must say that audit and security records are retained for a defined period after termination. If customers' contracts currently promise deletion of all data, this exception needs a contract amendment or a clear data-processing addendum, not just an internal policy.

**Backups: 35 days.** Backups exist for disaster recovery, and 90 days of dailies is more than most recovery scenarios need. Thirty-five days gives a month of rollback plus a few days of slack for detecting a slow-burning corruption. Cutting to 35 days means any deleted customer's data disappears from backups within 35 days of the live deletion, so total worst-case time to complete erasure is roughly 30 days (live) plus 35 days (backup expiry). If you want to hold the strict 30-day line, set backup retention to 30 days and delete live data at day zero to day 30 of termination; the data then leaves backups by day 60 at the outside. Decide which figure you can live with and write it into the contract.

**How the 30-day promise is kept.** Live systems: on termination, schedule a tenant-scoped deletion job that removes the customer's rows, files, search indexes and caches within the 30 days, and writes an audit record. Logs: they expire on their own schedule inside 30 days. Backups: you generally cannot surgically remove one tenant from a snapshot, so rely on short expiry and say so. The regulator-friendly position, reflected in data protection authority guidance and the idea of putting data 'beyond use', is that backed-up data is not actively processed, is protected, and is overwritten on a fixed cycle. Two rules make that true: never restore a backup into production without re-running the deletion ledger (keep a ledger of terminated tenants and replay it after any restore), and tell customers in the contract that backup copies persist for up to N days after deletion. Do not claim instant or total erasure; claim deletion from live systems within 30 days and expiry from backups within a stated period.

**Automatic enforcement.** Use storage-level lifecycle rules rather than cron scripts: object-store lifecycle policies on log buckets (30-day expiry; 13-month for the audit bucket), log platform retention settings per index, and backup retention set in the backup service itself. Make the audit bucket write-once or append-only with restricted delete rights so that retention is enforced by the platform and tampering is hard. Define everything in infrastructure-as-code so the schedule lives in version control and changes go through review.

**Proving it ran.** Three artefacts. First, exported configuration snapshots (or IaC state) showing the retention rules, captured monthly. Second, a monthly automated check that lists the oldest object or record in each class and fails an alert if any exceeds its limit by a margin; store the output. Third, a deletion ledger: each tenant-termination job writes a record with tenant ID, timestamps, and counts of deleted items. Keep these evidence records themselves free of personal data. Review them in a short monthly ritual owned by one named engineer.

**GDPR concepts relied on, stated carefully.** Storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)): personal data kept no longer than necessary for its purpose, which is why each class has a stated purpose and period. Data minimisation (Art. 5(1)(c)): the reason to stop logging free text and to keep audit logs narrow. Security of processing (Art. 32) and accountability (Art. 5(2)): the basis for keeping audit logs and for documenting and evidencing the schedule. Processor role (Art. 28): for customer data, the company is likely a processor, so it acts on the controller's documented instructions, and the contract's deletion terms are those instructions; Art. 28(3)(g) requires deleting or returning data at the end of services unless law requires storage. Erasure (Art. 17) is a data-subject right against controllers and is not the same as the contractual deletion promise. Not claimed: that this policy guarantees compliance, that truncated IPs are anonymous, or that backups are exempt from GDPR.

**Open questions.** Does counsel accept 13 months for audit logs and the backup residual period? Do any US customers or sectors impose their own retention rules? Do any contracts promise stricter terms than 30 days? Are there legal holds or litigation scenarios that must override automatic deletion? Resolve these before publishing the schedule.
